reading.title: Sending Signals Into the Sky
reading.purpose: Explore how weather teams launch high-altitude balloons and probes using the roots mit and miss.
paras: Twice a day, weather crews around the world launch tall balloons into the sky. Each flight has one clear mission: gather temperature, wind, and air-pressure data miles above the ground. The root miss comes from a Latin word meaning "to send." The whole project is about sending tools up and getting signals back.

Before a launch, crews must submit a flight plan to air-traffic officials. Those officials check the route and permit the balloon to rise only when the sky is clear. Sometimes a lab accepts a special commission from a city to track big storms all season.

Under the latex balloon hangs a small foam box called a radiosonde. It is not like a military missile built as a launched weapon. Instead, this light box holds tiny sensors and a small radio. As it climbs, the box begins to emit steady radio pulses, sending data back to a ground antenna every second.

High winds and icy clouds can make those signals intermittent, stopping and starting again as the balloon spins in a storm. Crews never dismiss a shaky reading without checking it. Even a brief drop in pressure can warn of shifting weather.

Field crews must commit to working in rain, heat, or cold dawn air until the flight ends. When a sensor fails, they admit the error and fix the wires. Then they prep the next balloon so forecasters can trust each report.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "intermittent" most nearly means
choices: too weak to reach a ground antenna from the sky
stopping and starting again instead of staying steady
sent only twice a day during calm, sunny mornings
approved by aviation officials before a balloon launch
qs.why: Paragraph 4 defines intermittent right after the comma as "stopping and starting again as the balloon tumbles."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how a radiosonde sends data back to scientists on the ground?
choices: Before a launch, crews must submit a flight plan to air-traffic officials.
Under the latex balloon hangs a small foam box called a radiosonde.
As it climbs, the box begins to emit steady radio pulses, sending data back to a ground antenna every second.
Field crews must commit to working in rain, heat, or cold dawn air until the flight ends.
qs.why: This sentence explains that the radiosonde emits steady radio pulses to a ground antenna every second.

ev.text: As it climbs, the box begins to emit steady radio pulses, sending data back to a ground antenna every second.

qs.q: Why do crews check shaky radio readings instead of throwing them away?
choices: Because air-traffic officials fine stations that lose a small foam box.
Because even a short signal might warn of a weather shift.
Because weather balloons can only be launched once during a whole season.
Because every radiosonde is heavier and costlier than a large rocket.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 states that "even a brief dip in pressure can warn of shifting weather."

qs.q: What is this reading mostly about?
choices: How weather crews plan, launch, and track high-altitude balloon flights.
Why aviation officials prefer launching balloons during freezing dawn air.
How military rockets differ from foam boxes carried by latex balloons.
Why universities pay meteorologists to study icy clouds in winter.
qs.why: From planning and permits to radiosonde signals and crew dedication, the passage explains how weather-balloon missions work.

sending data back to a ground antenna
